copies.headline: Uncut Cokerr Does It Again, Obviously
copies.body:
Of course Adam gets an A+. Of course he does. This is a man who broke his own #1 seed curse last year and then treated this draft like a victory lap nobody asked him to take. JSN at 7 is clean value, Bucky Irving six spots early is a bet on volume that already looks smart, and then he just starts stealing quarterbacks for sport — Jayden Daniels drops into round 7, thirty-eight picks past where he should go, and Adam's sitting there with a league-winning QB1 as a luxury. Then he does it again in round 12 with Brock Purdy. That's not a QB room, that's a hedge fund.
The RB corps is thin and the WR3-4 range is replacement-level filler, hence the gentlemen's-C there, but Sam LaPorta plus Mark Andrews at TE is absurd security. Consistent, relentless, allergic to punting anything. 34-22 for a reason. The rest of you are drafting to keep up.

copies.headline: The Aura Farm Bought Every WR in Sight
copies.body:
CeeDee Lamb at 11, DeVonta Smith falling into round 4, Jameson Williams eight spots late, then Khalil Shakir basically for free in round 11 — this is what a receiver corps looks like when someone refuses to blink. The RB room is quietly excellent too, Chase Brown and Travis Etienne as a 1-2 punch with Bhayshul Tuten and Dylan Sampson stashed as lottery tickets, and George Kittle at pick 86 is the single best value anybody got at the cabin this year. Deebo in round 9 was a real reach, but at that price it barely dents the grade.
The QB room is the one hole, Trevor Lawrence and Jordan Love as a plan that only works if both hit, which is why the letter grade caps at A instead of A+. Very on-brand for a guy whose seasons alternate between 10-4 and 4-10 like a light switch — all the ceiling in the world, and a floor that depends entirely on quarterback health.

copies.headline: Rezac Builds A Backfield, Prays For The Rest
copies.body:
Logan actually drafted like a man who remembers last year's dress. Saquon Barkley at 15 and Jeremiyah Love falling into his lap twelve picks late gives him the best one-two punch at RB in this league, full stop, and grabbing Jalen Hurts nineteen picks past his normal price in round six is the kind of value that makes the rest of us check the wire out of spite. Justin Jefferson anchors the WR room fine, but everything after him is a shrug — Tetairoa McMillan and Luther Burden are lottery tickets, Pittman and Worthy are floor plays, and the tight end room is Isaiah Likely and a prayer.
The RB A carries this to a B almost by itself, which tracks for a guy whose whole fantasy identity is loading one position and hoping the rest sorts itself out in-season. That's also just Logan: great on paper in August, terrible in January. Two straight number-one seeds and zero playoff wins to show for it. The backfield is genuinely elite. Whether it survives the choke is the only question that's ever mattered with him.

copies.headline: The Backfield's Loaded, The Rest Is a Rumor
copies.body:
Noah did what Noah does: build the engine and worry about the trim later. James Cook and De'Von Achane at the top gives him the best RB room in the league by a mile, and stealing Rhamondre Stevenson in round 7 and Tyjae Spears in round 12 means he's got bailouts if either stud misses time. Garrett Wilson and Mike Evans anchor a solid WR corps, and grabbing Drake Maye seventeen spots early for a QB1 you don't have to think about again is exactly the kind of quiet value that never shows up in the recap headlines. The tradeoff is Colston Loveland and Brenton Strange, which isn't a tight end room so much as a waiver-wire waiting list — that's the one hole opponents will actually attack him through.
Nobody drafts Noah seriously in August, and that's the joke at this point — a 7 seed title and five playoff wins says the man doesn't need your respect, just your playoff spot. This roster is heavy where it matters and thin where he's betting you won't notice. History says don't bet against it.

copies.headline: Burrowed Treasure Forgot to Draft a Team Name
copies.body:
CJ built this draft like a man who read a WR scarcity article at 2am and panicked well. Jonathan Taylor at 9 is fine, on-market, no complaints, but then he reached for Quinshon Judkins seventeen spots early in round 3 and buried what should've been his best position under a pile of TreVeyon Henderson, Chuba Hubbard, Isiah Pacheco and Zach Charbonnet — that's not a running back room, that's a waiting room. Meanwhile the WR corps is legitimately great: Rashee Rice, Emeka Egbuka, Parker Washington, Alec Pierce all came in at or below market. Joe Burrow falling to round 6 is the one true heist of this whole draft, +21 value, and CJ deserves credit for not overthinking it.
Which is the CJ experience in a nutshell — one brilliant read surrounded by a defense that can't stop the run. One winning season in four years, and this roster has the same shape: a great secondary, no front seven. C-plus feels generous.

copies.headline: Two Tight Ends, Zero Wide Receiver Plan
copies.body:
Puka Nacua at 1.04 is fine, unspectacular, exactly what a top-four pick should be. Then John gets cute: Brock Bowers and Trey McBride back to back gives him the best tight end room in the league and no earthly reason to have done that, since one elite tight end already solves the position. Kyren Williams at 45 is a legitimate heist, the best value on his whole board, but he buried it by reaching for Brian Thomas Jr. two rounds later at a 22-spot markup right as the wideout depth chart got murky in Jacksonville. The WR room after Puka is D'Andre Swift's backfield mate energy — Quentin Johnston, Makai Lemon, Jauan Jennings, names you plug in and hope.
This is peak John: overthink the middle rounds, undervalue the position that actually wins leagues, still somehow finish 6th. Ten-and-four a year ago, still no ring, still chasing Peter at 6-3 head-to-head like it means something. The Stafford flier at 148 for +40 value is the one round-15 lottery ticket that might actually cash. Everything else here is a shrug.

copies.headline: Chase Went First, Then Isaac Panicked
copies.body:
Ja'Marr Chase at 3 is a gift, no complaints there. Then Isaac spent the next thirteen rounds trying to talk himself into a receiver room so deep it becomes shallow — Nabers, McLaurin, Metcalf, Wan'Dale, Meyers, Adonai Mitchell, all serviceable, none of them separating, and the room grades out an F because you cannot roster six WR2s and call it a strategy. The RB corps is the actual save here, with Javonte Williams overdrafted by a round but Skattebo at 51 quietly the best pick on the entire roster. Bo Nix forty spots early at QB is the kind of reach that only makes sense if you've already given up on the position, which, given Malik Willis as the backup plan, tracks.
This is a team built by someone still chasing 11-3 in 2022, grabbing name value at every turn instead of asking what the roster needs. Hockenson and Kincaid give you a real TE room, which is nice, but it doesn't fix a WR corps that's all floor and no ceiling. Seventh place feels generous.

copies.headline: Gibbs Was the Plan, Then the Plan Died
copies.body:
Jahmyr Gibbs at 1.1 is the correct start to any draft, and Nico Collins in round two is legitimate value. Then Mitchell's board seems to catch fire. Josh Jacobs nine slots early, DJ Moore six early, Rachaad White reached by fourteen picks in round nine — that's not building a roster, that's panic-buying running backs you already have enough of. The QB room is the actual crime scene: Jaxson Dart and Daniel Jones as your answers is a tacit admission you forgot the position existed until round six, and it shows, hence the F. Tyler Warren early plus a 34-pick-late Travis Kelce steal salvages the tight end spot and is basically the only unit that looks planned rather than stumbled into.
This is peak Mitchell: no real identity, a few shrewd finds buried in a pile of reaches, ending up somewhere in the middle nobody remembers. Three 7-7 seasons in four years says this team finds a way to be fine no matter what the draft board says, and a D+ with Gibbs and Collins on it might just be fine again. Mr. .500 drafted like Mr. .500.

copies.headline: Lunchbox Built a Wax Museum Backfield
copies.body:
Christian McCaffrey and Derrick Henry going back to back in rounds one and two reads like a fantasy portfolio from 2023, and that's the problem — Leif spent premium capital on two running backs whose bodies have logged more mileage than the lake cabin itself. Josh Allen falling to him at pick 29 is a legitimate heist, and grabbing Mahomes as a QB2 in round 13 is downright greedy, but you can't win with a backfield built on nostalgia and an F-graded tight end room anchored by Kyle Pitts and Greg Dulcich, who at pick 188 is basically bye-week filler for a bye-week filler. Woody Marks 28 spots early sealed the RB room's fate.
The receiver corps is legitimately solid — Adams, Diggs, Harrison Jr., Reed gives him weekly floor — which is exactly why this lands at a D+ instead of an F. Classic Joey Lunchbox: quietly competent in flashes, structurally broken everywhere else, still finding new ways to finish 9th with a 22-34 career record intact.

copies.headline: Bijan, Two Quarterbacks, and a Void at RB2
copies.body:
Peter opened with the right idea and then argued himself out of it for ten rounds. Bijan Robinson at 1.2 is clean value, and the wideout trio of A.J. Brown, George Pickens and Tee Higgins gives him a receiving corps that can win weeks by itself. Then he grabbed Lamar Jackson at pick 50, twenty spots ahead of market, and doubled back for Dak Prescott in round 13 like the first quarterback might not show up. Great insurance policy, wrong things to insure. Meanwhile the RB room behind Bijan is Jonathon Brooks, Jordan Mason, Kyle Monangai and Chris Rodriguez — a stack of injury-and-role questions that reads like he punted the position on purpose. Tucker Kraft is fine, but the TE room dies there.
This is 2022 Peter in miniature: one unimpeachable superstar pick propping up a plan that doesn't survive contact with a bye week. He's got two franchise quarterbacks and no answer at RB2. The basement's still under construction.

copies.headline: The Cinderella Story That Forgot the WR Room
copies.body:
Ashton Jeanty and Breece Hall at the top is a legitimate RB core, the kind of foundation that wins you your division if literally nothing else goes wrong. Nothing else went right. Kaleb reached for Drake London and Ladd McConkey early, which was fine, then spent the next five rounds torching every ounce of goodwill by taking Carnell Tate nine spots early, Jordan Addison a full 24 spots early, and Keenan Allen 31 spots early — an entire receiving corps built on paying retail for players everyone else was getting at clearance prices. Harold Fannin and Kenyon Sadiq at TE is a tire fire nobody asked for. The one bright spot: Justin Herbert fell into his lap in round 8 at +20 value, which at least means the QB room isn't the problem.
This is peak Kaleb. Worst-to-first in 2023, three straight 8-6 seasons since, always circling relevance without landing it. This roster is Jeanty-or-bust, and the receiver room says bust.

copies.headline: Grant Reached For Everything Except A Quarterback
copies.body:
Amon-Ra at six was fine, Omarion Hampton a round early was fine, and then the wheels came off in a way that only Grant can manage. Zay Flowers nine spots early, Christian Watson nine spots early, Jacory Croskey-Merritt fifteen spots early, Tank Bigsby a full two rounds early — this is a man who saw the ADP sheet and decided it was a suggestion for other people. He built four wideouts he liked and zero running backs anyone else wanted, then waited until round 10 for his first quarterback and got Kyler Murray, whose legs are the only thing keeping this roster's floor above sea level. Dallas Goedert in round 11 is the one correct guess on the whole board, which is why TE is the lone letter grade that doesn't look like a ransom note.
This is peak Grant: no plan, no patience, and somehow still capable of a 9-5 season out of pure chaos energy. The board says disaster. History says don't rule it out.

intro: Mr. Consistent did it again — Adam somehow drafted like a man who's never lost, which, fine, he basically hasn't, and the A+ makes it official that boring and great are the same thing in his hands. Christian wasn't far behind, but the real story is the middle class of B's and C's who played it safe while Peter and Kaleb torched their own rosters like it's 2023 all over again. Grant's F somehow finds a new floor, which given last place gets a dress at the cabin should have him nervous already. Logan grading out fine here means nothing — dude's taken the 1-seed to the graveyard twice, so a good draft is just a good ghost story so far.
